summary:
Mozambique's legal position is among the more permissive in sub-Saharan Africa. The 2015 Penal Code removed the colonial-era 'vices against nature' provision, and same-sex conduct has been legal since. A trans visitor faces no criminal exposure on the basis of consensual conduct or identity.

There is no procedure for legal gender recognition. A visitor whose passport or other documents carry markers inconsistent with their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible at checkpoints and in any interaction requiring identification; the sources do not describe a formal screening process, but they also provide no assurance against one.

Protection machinery exists in limited form. After applications blocked from 2008 onward, the Constitutional Council ruled on 28 November 2017 that the status of Lambda Mozambique did not violate the constitution, unblocking registration of the country's only LGBTIQ organisation. Lambda had previously operated unregistered and pivoted to anti-discrimination lobbying after the 2015 Penal Code.

There is no documented pattern of police targeting of LGBTIQ people. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 records general police detentions and election-related arrests but contains no transgender-specific findings. Lambda's Carina Capitine stated in 2015 that the LGBT community is not targeted by violence as in some African countries, while still facing discrimination.

Counterweights are substantial. No SOGI hate-crime statute is in force. Societal attitudes are broadly neutral at the aggregate level, but LGBTIQ people encounter family ostracisation and barriers in employment and education, and social hostility outside Maputo is significant. The 2024 opposition pledge by PODEMOS raised community expectations and then disappointed them.

For a visitor: no legal exposure from identity or conduct, modest support infrastructure concentrated in the capital, and no legal route to have documents corrected before travel.
tangentialFactors:
The Cabo Delgado insurgency affects the north of the country. This is a general security risk rather than a trans-specific one, but it shapes where a visitor can move safely.

Attitudinal data place Mozambique at the more tolerant end of the region. Afrobarometer reporting cited in March 2016 found 56% of respondents would welcome or not be bothered by a homosexual neighbour, against 5% in Uganda, Burkina Faso and Niger. Aggregate tolerance of this kind does not translate into legal protection, and it does not measure attitudes toward trans people specifically.

The 2024 electoral cycle produced turbulence in the community's expectations: an opposition pledge by PODEMOS was taken as a signal of change and did not deliver. Political commitments of this kind should not be read as enacted law.
localsOnly:
The 2024 penal code removed an employment non-discrimination protection that had previously existed. Residents lose a formal recourse that was on the books before it.

LGBTIQ residents face family ostracisation and barriers in employment and education, even where societal attitudes are described as broadly neutral. Discrimination rather than violence is the pattern reported by community figures.

Lambda Mozambique operates as the country's only LGBTIQ organisation, its legal status settled by the Constitutional Council in November 2017 after a decade of blocked registration attempts dating from 2008.

Organising has a long local history: a first newspaper article arguing gay rights appeared in Agencia de Informacao on 7 July 2006, Maputo men petitioned parliament, and the group remained unregistered as of March 2011 while working under the colonial-era law that was not repealed until 2015.
outOfScopeNotes:
The HRW World Report 2024 Mozambique chapter, published 11 January 2024, gives no transgender-specific content and no information on how trans prisoners are housed. Prison-placement treatment for trans detainees is unresolved on this inventory.

No source in the inventory addresses visa rules, border screening, or entry documentation requirements as they apply to trans travellers. Whether any such screening occurs is not sourced either way.

The status and scope of hate-crime protection for SOGI-motivated offences is carried from the prior assessment and is not independently sourced here; the inventory contains no statute or case on point.

The claim that the 2024 penal code removed the employment non-discrimination protection comes from a single source (Outright International, updated March 2026). The provision's prior wording, the effective date, and whether any replacement remedy exists are unresolved.

Societal-attitude figures derive from Afrobarometer as republished in March 2016 and measure attitudes to homosexuality, not to trans people, and not to current conditions.
